**Answer: Yes, $g(x)$ is necessarily the zero function.**

**Proof.**

Make the substitution $t = \cos x$. Since $\cos$ is a strictly decreasing bijection $[0,\pi]\to[-1,1]$, we have $x=\arccos t$ and $dx = -dt/\sqrt{1-t^{2}}$. The given condition becomes, for every polynomial $H$,

$$\int_{0}^{\pi} g(x)\,H(\cos x)\,dx \;=\; \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{g(\arccos t)}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}\,H(t)\,dt \;=\; 0.$$

Define
$$f(t) \;=\; \frac{g(\arccos t)}{\sqrt{1-t^{2}}}, \qquad t\in(-1,1).$$

Because $g$ is continuous on $[0,\pi]$ and $\arccos$ is continuous, $g(\arccos t)$ is continuous (hence bounded) on $[-1,1]$. The factor $1/\sqrt{1-t^{2}}$ is integrable on $(-1,1)$ (it is the Chebyshev weight, with $\int_{-1}^{1}(1-t^{2})^{-1/2}dt=\pi<\infty$). Thus $f\in L^{1}(-1,1)$, and the hypothesis reads

$$\int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\,H(t)\,dt = 0 \qquad\text{for every polynomial } H.$$

By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, polynomials are dense in $C[-1,1]$ under the supremum norm. For any $\varphi\in C[-1,1]$, choose polynomials $H_n\to\varphi$ uniformly. Since $f\in L^{1}$ and $\varphi$ is bounded,

$$\left|\int_{-1}^{1} f\,(H_n-\varphi)\,dt\right| \;\le\; \|H_n-\varphi\|_{\infty}\int_{-1}^{1}|f|\,dt \;\longrightarrow\; 0.$$

Hence $\int_{-1}^{1} f(t)\,\varphi(t)\,dt = 0$ for every $\varphi\in C[-1,1]$.

By the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (a continuous linear functional on $C[-1,1]$ represented by an $L^{1}$ density that annihilates all continuous functions must be the zero density), $f=0$ almost everywhere on $(-1,1)$.

Since $\sqrt{1-t^{2}}>0$ on $(-1,1)$, this gives $g(\arccos t)=0$ for almost every $t\in(-1,1)$.

The map $\arccos:(-1,1)\to(0,\pi)$ is a smooth diffeomorphism with nowhere-vanishing derivative, so it maps null sets to null sets. Therefore $g(x)=0$ for almost every $x\in(0,\pi)$.

Finally, $g$ is continuous on $[0,\pi]$. A continuous function that vanishes almost everywhere must vanish everywhere: if $g(x_0)\neq 0$ for some $x_0$, continuity gives a neighborhood of $x_0$ on which $|g|>0$, and that neighborhood has positive measure—a contradiction.

Therefore $g\equiv 0$ on $[0,\pi]$. $\blacksquare$
